title: Higher-order functions and callbacks as values
hook: A higher-order function takes another function as an argument or returns one. That is how map, filter, middleware, and debounce are built — and why JavaScript treats callbacks as first-class values.

blocks.text: A **higher-order function** (HOF) is any function that operates on other functions: it accepts a callback, returns a new function, or both. Because functions are objects in JavaScript, you pass them like any other value. **Callbacks** are functions you pass to be invoked later — by array methods, event emitters, or timers. Combining HOFs with closures lets you specialize behavior without subclassing.

entries.plainDefinition: A function that takes and/or returns another function.
A function passed to another function to run at a later time or on an event.
Functions can be assigned, passed, returned, and stored — not just declared and called.
Fixing some arguments of a function to produce a narrower function.

blocks.text: Higher-order functions are the backbone of functional JavaScript: `Array.prototype.map`, Express middleware, `addEventListener`, and React hooks all rely on passing functions. Interviewers ask you to implement `once`, `memoize`, or `debounce` — each is a HOF returning a closure. Misunderstanding when the inner function runs (sync vs async) and what it captures causes bugs in production API clients and UI event handlers.

blocks.title: Return functions for configuration
blocks.body: const withAuth = (token) => (url) => fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: token } }); — outer HOF configures, inner closure executes.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Pass function reference
items.body: Caller supplies a callback — not invoked yet, just a value.

items.title: HOF stores or schedules it
items.body: May call immediately (map), later (setTimeout), or on event (click).

items.title: Invoke with arguments
items.body: HOF controls what arguments the callback receives — element, index, event object.

items.title: Return new function (optional)
items.body: Factory HOFs return specialized closures sharing captured config.

diagram.title: Higher-order function flow
diagram.source:
flowchart LR

  H --> I{When?}

  I -->|later| T[schedule fn]
  H --> R[return specialized fn]

blocks.title: Invoking the callback immediately when you meant to pass it
blocks.body: onClick={handler()} calls now and passes the return value. Correct: onClick={handler} or onClick={() => handler(id)}.

blocks.title: Forgetting this binding in returned methods
blocks.body: Returning a method extracted from an object loses this unless bound or wrapped in an arrow in the right scope.

blocks.text: Interview implementations: debounce (reset timer on each call), throttle (max one call per window), memoize (cache by serialized args), concurrency-limited Promise pool (queue + active count). Production proof: debounce on search input — Network tab should show one request per pause, not per keystroke. A memoize that captures unbounded argument keys leaks memory; use LRU or WeakMap when keys are objects. HOFs that register listeners must return an unsubscribe function — same pattern as AbortSignal.

snippet.label: debounce — failure mode without cleanup
snippet.explanation: Line 1: HOF returns closure over timer id. Line 10: production must cancel pending timer on unmount — interviewers ask about cleanup.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Pending timer on unmount; leading vs trailing edge
Dropped events at end of burst
Unbounded cache; stale results if inputs mutate
Shared mutable attempt counter across parallel calls

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Implementing debounce with Date.now polling instead of clearTimeout/setTimeout. Not explaining that the returned function is a closure holding timer state. Saying map mutates the array. Unable to implement once without a global variable. Ignoring cleanup when the HOF schedules async work.

interviewTakeaways: Higher-order function = accepts and/or returns functions; callbacks are invoked by the HOF on its schedule.
once, debounce, memoize are standard closure + HOF interview implementations.
Pass function references, do not call early: onClick={fn} not onClick={fn()} unless intentional.
60s: Functions are first-class. HOFs configure behavior via returned closures. Debounce delays until quiet; throttle caps rate. Always consider timer/listener cleanup.
Follow-up: implement debounce with leading edge option or memoize with LRU cap.
commonPitfalls: Calling the callback when registering: addEventListener('click', handler()) — wrong.
Shared mutable state in a retry HOF used concurrently — race on attempt count.
Strong answer: 'HOF passes or returns functions. Closures hold config. Debounce/throttle/once are closure factories. Profile network and clear timers on teardown.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# methods become HOF arguments via Func/Action. JavaScript needs no conversion — functions are already objects.
TypeScript can type map as map<T,U>(fn: (v:T)=>U): U[]. Callback parameters get full inference.
